topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: Bridging the AI literacy gap: mixed-methods evidence from employers on workforce readiness and curriculum priorities - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Bridging the AI literacy gap: mixed-methods evidence from employers on workforce readiness and curriculum priorities  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited clarity from title/snippet alone — appears to survey employers on AI literacy priorities, but geographic scope, sample size, and sector representation are unclear. Findings likely most applicable to sectors and regions represented in the employer sample.
takeaways: Identify specific AI literacy gaps your workforce faces by benchmarking against employer priorities documented in this research — this can guide targeted upskilling programmes.
Use curriculum priorities identified by employers to shape internal training design, ensuring your AI capability-building aligns with what organisations actually need rather than generic skills.
Assess readiness levels across your team using employer-informed benchmarks to segment employees into appropriate learning pathways rather than one-size-fits-all approaches.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European public health context; frameworks and competencies may have limited direct applicability to other sectors or non-European healthcare systems, though core digital literacy principles may transfer.
takeaways: Review identifies specific competency clusters (technical, data, governance, change management) that can inform design of AI literacy programs tailored to public health professionals rather than generic IT training.

European focus means regulatory context (GDPR, medical device regulations) differs from Australia — Australian organizations should map identified competencies against local privacy and health sector governance requirements before implementation.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on middle school education context. Applicability to adult workforce development and organisational settings requires careful adaptation, as cognitive development, learning environments, and motivational factors differ significantly between adolescents and working professionals.
takeaways: AI literacy frameworks should integrate technical skills (prompt engineering, data interpretation) with critical thinking components (bias recognition, ethical reasoning) rather than treating them as separate competencies — this holistic approach is foundational before employees can apply AI effectively in workplace contexts.

Scaffolding and progressive skill-building (starting with foundational concepts before advanced applications) improves retention and confidence — consider designing staged AI upskilling programs for employees rather than overwhelming them with comprehensive training.

Digital literacy frameworks must address not just tool use but conceptual understanding of how AI systems work and their limitations — this metacognitive layer is essential for employees to make sound judgement calls when deploying AI in real work situations.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on faculty development in public health academia, findings may not generalise to other sectors or non-academic settings. Geographic scope and specific institutions not detailed in snippet.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI literacy is addressable through structured professional development; organisations should invest in tailored training programmes that move staff from resistance to readiness rather than assuming capability or willingness.

Public health educators need targeted AI literacy development to effectively teach AI concepts to their students — this suggests that upskilling current workforce is a prerequisite before scaling AI capabilities across organisations.
Change management matters: framing AI literacy as a faculty development priority (rather than a technical mandate) may increase engagement and reduce implementation barriers.

articles.title: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey analysis typically draws on global client data and industry trends, but specific recommendations may reflect practices most common in large organisations and developed economies. Applicability to Australian small-to-medium enterprises or public sector may vary.
takeaways: Identify which roles in your team will be most disrupted by generative AI and prioritise reskilling programs for those cohorts first, rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.

Design upskilling pathways that combine technical AI literacy (prompt engineering, tool use) with complementary soft skills like critical thinking and change management, since technical skills alone won't sustain competitive advantage.

Create clear progression tracks that show employees how learning AI capabilities connects to career development and job security, to increase engagement and reduce resistance to reskilling initiatives.

articles.title: Fostering AI literacy in pre-service teachers: impact of a training intervention on awareness, attitude and trust in AI - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Fostering AI literacy in pre-service teachers: impact of a training intervention on awareness, attitude and trust in AI  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited to pre-service teachers; findings may not generalise to experienced educators or non-teaching professionals. Sample characteristics, geographic location, and intervention duration not evident from title/snippet, restricting broader applicability.
takeaways: Structured AI literacy training can measurably improve teachers' awareness, attitudes, and trust in AI tools—suggesting similar interventions could work for other professional groups developing AI capabilities.
Target awareness, attitudes, and trust as distinct but interconnected outcomes when designing AI literacy programmes, rather than focusing on knowledge alone.

Early intervention with pre-service teachers may be more effective than post-hoc training; consider building AI literacy into initial professional preparation rather than relying on in-service upskilling.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Cannot assess from snippet alone — full article details needed. Generalisability likely depends on sample size, sectors studied, and geographic scope, which are not provided in the title or snippet.
takeaways: AI adoption in organisations may have paradoxical effects on creativity — it can both enhance and inhibit creative output depending on implementation context and how employees perceive autonomy vs. control.
When introducing AI tools, clarify how they complement (rather than replace) human creative thinking, and monitor whether employees feel empowered or constrained by AI-assisted workflows.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited until full article reviewed. The focus on 'paternalistic leadership' suggests data likely from East Asian organisational contexts where this leadership style is more prevalent; findings may not generalise to Western decentralised management structures common in Australian workplaces.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools by involving employees in customising and 'crafting' how AI is integrated into their work — this increases collaboration and reduces resistance regardless of leadership style.

Under paternalistic leadership contexts, emphasise mentorship and guidance around AI adoption to strengthen the ownership-collaboration link; in Australian settings, consider how to adapt this insight for flatter hierarchies by framing AI customisation as autonomy-enhancing rather than directive.

Assess your organisation's leadership culture before rolling out AI initiatives — the pathway from ownership to collaboration may differ significantly between paternalistic and participative management models.

articles.title: Corporate sustainability and artificial intelligence-enabled workforce transformation: a dual-pathway model of employee capability, empowerment, anxiety, and job insecurity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Corporate sustainability and artificial intelligence-enabled workforce transformation: a dual-pathway model of employee capability, empowerment, anxiety, and job insecurity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The dual-pathway model may apply broadly to organisations undergoing AI-enabled transformation, but geographic scope, sector diversity, and sample size are unclear.
takeaways: AI transformation initiatives should address both capability development and psychological safety together — focusing on upskilling alone without managing anxiety and job insecurity may undermine engagement and empowerment.

Design interventions that build employee agency and control over AI adoption; the model suggests empowerment may be a key mechanism to mitigate job insecurity concerns during workforce transformation.
Monitor and measure both capability gains and psychological outcomes (anxiety, insecurity) as interdependent indicators of transformation success, not just technical adoption metrics.

articles.title: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear — the snippet provides insufficient detail about sample size, geography, sectors, or methodology. Full article review needed to assess scope and applicability.
takeaways: Generative AI can create a paradox where automation of knowledge tasks reduces employee engagement with learning, while augmentation features (e.g., suggestions, tools) can enhance knowledge-building — understanding which effect dominates in your context is critical for implementation strategy.

Consider designing AI tools to emphasise augmentation (supporting existing work) rather than pure automation (replacing tasks) if your goal is to maintain or develop employee knowledge capabilities alongside efficiency gains.

articles.title: Worried about AI in the workplace? You’re not alone - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Worried about AI in the workplace? You’re not alone  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Limited — reflects American workforce concerns and APA membership perspectives; may not generalise to Australian workplace contexts, which have different regulatory frameworks (Fair Work Act), cultural attitudes toward technology, and labour market conditions.
takeaways: Acknowledge that AI-related workplace anxiety is widespread among employees; use this as a starting point for psychological safety conversations rather than dismissing concerns as outlier views.

Consider designing targeted communication and upskilling programs that address specific anxieties about AI displacement, skill obsolescence, and job security — these appear to be shared concerns worth addressing proactively.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The theoretical model (AI adoption → psychological safety → depression) may apply across sectors, but findings could be limited by sample geography, industry type, and organisational context.
takeaways: Psychological safety is a critical mediator between AI adoption and employee wellbeing—prioritise creating environments where staff feel safe raising concerns about AI implementation, not just technical rollout success.

Ethical leadership during AI adoption is protective against depression and disengagement; leaders must visibly model ethical reasoning about AI use, acknowledge risks, and involve employees in decisions about how AI affects their roles.

Monitor employee mental health proactively during AI transitions; depression may emerge not from AI itself but from feeling unsafe or unheard about its impact—screen for these psychological factors alongside technical adoption metrics.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte practitioner insights are based on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific case details and sample composition are not disclosed. Applicability may vary depending on organisational context and industry.
takeaways: Shift from treating AI adoption as a one-time implementation event to viewing it as an ongoing adaptation process requiring sustained behaviour change — this requires phased interventions beyond initial training.

Design change programmes that explicitly target the human behaviours needed for AI success (e.g., collaboration, comfort with ambiguity, continuous learning) rather than focusing only on technical skills or system features.

Identify and address psychological barriers early — resistance often stems from unclear role expectations and loss of autonomy rather than capability gaps, so diagnosis should precede intervention design.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on BCG's consulting experience across clients, but specific case studies and organisational contexts are not detailed in the snippet provided. Findings may reflect larger organisations with resources for transformation initiatives.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a workforce capability challenge, not just a technology implementation — prioritise upskilling and role redesign alongside tool deployment to drive genuine behaviour change.

Design change management strategies that address workforce concerns about AI (job security, skill obsolescence) explicitly, as these are primary barriers to adoption and engagement in transformation programs.

Build internal communication plans that connect AI implementation to tangible employee benefits — clearer career pathways, reduced routine work, skill development opportunities — to shift mindsets from resistance to participation.

articles.title: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience across sectors, but specific implementation details may need adaptation for Australian regulatory context and labour market conditions.
takeaways: Frame AI capability development as organisational change, not just skills training — this positions it as a strategic priority requiring leadership commitment and cultural shifts, not an isolated L&D initiative.
Design upskilling programmes to address resistance and mindset barriers alongside technical knowledge, using change management principles to increase adoption and sustained behaviour change.
Align AI upskilling timelines with organisational transformation roadmaps to create urgency and demonstrate how individual learning contributes to measurable business outcomes.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without empirical data or defined sample. Findings may reflect US-centric business school viewpoint and may not generalise to Australian organisational contexts or non-Anglo workforces.
takeaways: Identify which job roles in your organisation are most likely to be augmented or displaced by AI, then design targeted upskilling programmes for affected employees before disruption occurs.
Use AI adoption as a trigger to revisit performance management and incentive structures — ensure reward systems encourage collaboration with AI tools rather than resistance to them.

articles.title: The mental health implications of artificial intelligence adoption: the crucial role of self-efficacy - Nature
articles.snippet: The mental health implications of artificial intelligence adoption: the crucial role of self-efficacy  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed without access to full article methods; depends on sample size, geographic scope, and sector coverage. Flag to verify study design and participant demographics.
takeaways: Build self-efficacy through structured AI training and skill-building before deployment to protect employee mental health during AI adoption.
Monitor mental health outcomes (anxiety, stress, confidence) during AI implementation, particularly for employees with lower baseline AI self-efficacy, as a key risk factor for wellbeing.
Design change management interventions that explicitly address confidence and competence gaps — not just technical skill gaps — to support psychological adjustment to AI tools.

articles.title: The innovation paradox in human-AI symbiosis: ambidextrous effects of AI technology adoption on innovative behavior - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The innovation paradox in human-AI symbiosis: ambidextrous effects of AI technology adoption on innovative behavior  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from title and snippet alone — full text would be needed to assess sample size, sector coverage, and geographic scope.
takeaways: AI adoption may paradoxically reduce some forms of innovation (e.g., exploratory or divergent thinking) while enhancing others (e.g., execution or incremental improvement) — recognise this trade-off when designing AI rollouts.
When introducing AI tools, explicitly manage the risk that employees become over-reliant on AI-suggested solutions; build in practices that preserve human creative questioning and experimentation.

Design AI adoption programmes with awareness that the same technology can both enable and constrain innovation depending on how teams use it — training and work redesign matter as much as the tool itself.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: The science of why friendships keep us healthy - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: The science of why friendships keep us healthy  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: High — draws on established psychological research across multiple populations and health domains.
takeaways: Strong friendships have measurable biological effects: people with close social ties show better immune function, lower inflammation, and even longer lifespans — making friendship literally a health intervention.

Quality matters far more than quantity — a few deeply connected relationships provide greater health benefits than a large network of superficial contacts, challenging the notion that more friends always means better outcomes.
Social connection activates the same neural reward systems as food and money, explaining why loneliness physically hurts and why humans will go to extraordinary lengths to maintain relationships.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: Likely broad — music preference research typically draws from diverse international populations, though specific sample composition not detailed in snippet.
takeaways: Your taste in music genuinely reveals something universal about your personality — people with similar traits gravitate toward the same genres worldwide, suggesting personality shapes musical preference in a surprisingly consistent way.

This cuts across cultural and geographic boundaries in ways that challenge the idea that music taste is purely learned or culturally determined — there's something deeper linking who you are to what you listen to.
If you've ever bonded with someone over unexpected shared music taste, there might be a hidden personality match happening — your playlist could be a surprisingly accurate personality signal.

articles.title: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026 - Wiley & Sons
articles.snippet: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026  Wiley & Sons
articles.generalisability: Moderate — synthesises psychological research on true crime consumption, but specific empirical scope and geographic coverage of reviewed studies not evident from title and snippet alone.
takeaways: True crime's psychological appeal likely stems from multiple motives: voyeuristic curiosity about dark human behaviour, a sense of control and safety when consuming real danger from a distance, and morbid fascination with how ordinary people become extraordinary.

The fact that millions voluntarily consume gruesome real-world cases for entertainment reveals something intriguing about human psychology — we're drawn to transgression and taboo precisely because they're forbidden, yet podcasts and documentaries let us explore them safely.

True crime fandom isn't just morbid entertainment; it may satisfy deep psychological needs around understanding risk, reconstructing social order after disorder, and testing our moral boundaries in a contained environment.

articles.title: Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized - Science Daily
articles.snippet: Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized  Science Daily
articles.generalisability: Limited — a news summary without access to the underlying study details, methodology, sample size, or geographic scope; the actual research generalisability cannot be assessed from this snippet alone.
takeaways: The finding challenges the traditional nature-vs-nurture debate by suggesting genetics play a larger role in personality than previously thought — a counterintuitive result that upends decades of behavioural science assumptions.

If personality traits are more hardwired than we believed, it raises interesting questions about how much we can really 'change ourselves' through effort — a humbling reminder that our quirks might be baked in deeper than self-help culture suggests.

This touches on a timeless human fascination: are we products of our genes or our choices? The finding leans heavily toward genes, making it an engaging conversation starter about identity and free will.

articles.title: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors? - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors?  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — reviews MBTI research across multiple studies but limited by the methodological quality and scope of underlying research on leadership prediction.
takeaways: Despite MBTI's popularity in corporate settings, the evidence for its ability to predict actual leadership behaviours is surprisingly weak — many organisations invest in it without strong scientific backing.

The gap between what people believe MBTI tells them about leadership (its perceived utility) and what it actually predicts is a fascinating example of how appealing personality frameworks can persist in workplaces even when empirical support is thin.

This research highlights a broader pattern: personality typing systems are more useful for self-reflection and team conversation starters than as predictive tools for real-world leadership performance.

articles.title: Which Personality Traits Are Most Important to Employers? - Association for Psychological Science – APS
articles.snippet: Which Personality Traits Are Most Important to Employers?  Association for Psychological Science – APS
articles.generalisability: Limited — the snippet provides insufficient detail about sample composition, geographic scope, or methodology to assess generalisability. Likely reflects employer perspectives in English-speaking contexts, but specific limitations cannot be determined from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Employers prioritise personality traits beyond raw intelligence — a finding that might surprise those who assume technical skills dominate hiring decisions.

The specific traits employers value most reveal what soft skills actually move the needle in real hiring contexts, offering insight into the gap between what job postings ask for and what organisations truly reward.
Understanding which personality dimensions employers care about exposes how workplace culture and team dynamics shape hiring more than many job candidates realise.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited information available from snippet alone — generalisability depends on study design, sample size, and geographic scope, which are not evident from the title and snippet provided.
takeaways: AI adoption can negatively impact employee mental health (depression) when psychological safety is low — prioritise creating psychologically safe environments before or alongside AI implementation.

Ethical leadership is a critical moderator of AI adoption outcomes — leaders who model ethical decision-making and transparency around AI use can buffer against negative psychological effects on staff.
When rolling out AI tools, assess and strengthen psychological safety first; employees need to feel safe raising concerns about AI impacts on their work without fear of consequences.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Limited — BCG report title suggests focus on organisational practices, but snippet provides insufficient detail on sample composition, geography, or methodology to assess generalisability. Likely reflects BCG client base (predominantly US and Western Europe), which may not reflect Australian workplace contexts.
takeaways: Psychological safety can reduce barriers to participation and voice across hierarchical or demographically diverse teams — consider auditing your team's norms around speaking up and mistake tolerance to identify where invisible hierarchies may silence contributions.

If psychological safety is framed as 'levelling the playing field,' explore how your current team practices (meeting dynamics, feedback processes, error handling) inadvertently advantage some voices over others and design interventions accordingly.

articles.title: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024 - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: US-focused findings on workplace psychological safety trends. Generalisability to Australian workplaces may be limited due to differences in employment law, workplace culture, and organisational practices between the US and Australia.
takeaways: Identify specific barriers to psychological safety in your team (e.g., fear of speaking up, exclusion from decision-making) using frameworks from the APA's Work in America research to tailor interventions.
Track psychological safety metrics alongside engagement and retention data to demonstrate business impact and secure leadership support for safety-focused initiatives.
Review how organisational changes (restructures, hybrid work, automation) are affecting team members' sense of safety and belonging, and adjust communication and support strategies accordingly.

articles.title: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience across sectors, but limited transparency on sample composition, methodology, and geographic distribution of case studies.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as expanding employee agency rather than automation threat — this psychological reframing can reduce defensive behaviours and build psychological safety around AI tools.
Design AI implementation processes that explicitly involve employees in defining how tools will be used in their roles, creating shared ownership and reducing fear of displacement.

Establish clear feedback loops and control mechanisms so employees feel they retain meaningful agency over their work when AI systems are involved — perceived loss of control undermines psychological safety.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026  PwC
articles.generalisability: Moderate to high — PwC's global workforce survey typically reaches thousands of respondents across multiple countries and sectors, though specific methodology details are not provided in the snippet. Results likely skew toward white-collar and professional sectors.
takeaways: Use survey findings to benchmark psychological safety concerns in your organisation against global trends, identifying whether your workplace's safety challenges are sector-wide or unique.

If the survey highlights specific fears (e.g., job security, AI impact, leadership trust), conduct focus groups or pulse surveys with your teams to understand how these global concerns manifest locally in your Melbourne workplace.

Share relevant anonymised survey insights with leadership to build the business case for psychological safety interventions, demonstrating that addressing these concerns is a competitive workforce retention issue.

articles.title: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams - SHRM
articles.snippet: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams  SHRM
articles.generalisability: Moderate — SHRM (US-based HR body) provides US-centric HR guidance. Principles of psychological safety are broadly applicable, but specific HR practices and regulatory context may differ in Australia.
takeaways: Identify the specific four leadership behaviours SHRM recommends (likely including modelling vulnerability, responding non-defensively to questions, and inviting input) and audit your own leadership team's current practice against these behaviours.

Implement a structured feedback mechanism where team members can raise concerns or ideas without fear of negative consequences, and visibly respond to and act on that feedback to demonstrate safety is genuine.
Create explicit norms around psychological safety in team charters or working agreements, then reinforce them consistently through how you handle mistakes, dissent, and interpersonal conflict.
